messages.author: 5e426c478a162ca8
messages.subject: negative binomial for non-integer counts
parts:
Hello again, I've heard it said in many different places that negative binomial distribution is not to be used with non-integer data, and yet this is obviously one of the more common suggestions in density surface modelling, where non-integer "counts" arise when there are detection covariates. Is this just the kind of thing where negative binomial is simply an approximation that can fit despite the data not being entirely by the rules? In the context of a paper, do you simply justify it with your model diagnostics? or is there theory that can be appealed to?

Thanks,
Kevin

messages.author: 1fb54f491646a589
messages.subject: RE: [distance-sampling] negative binomial for non-integer counts
parts:
Negative binomial and Poisson distributions are appropriate for modelling counts from distance sampling.  Probability of detection is addressed through an offset in the model.  That offset must be estimated.  But the model is still applied to integer counts.

 

Steve Buckland

OK – sorry.  I guess it would just be an ad hoc model if you use negative binomial in that case.  I might be more inclined to use a continuous distribution like gamma.  It is only when you have individual-specific covariates that you need to resort to this.  If the covariates apply to the line or point, or at a higher level, you can use the offset approach.

 

Steve

messages.author: 350dad0a615d36db
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] negative binomial for non-integer counts
parts:
Hi Kevin, hi listfolks,

Two quick things here:

1. you don't always need to use a Horvtiz-Thompson-ised response when
there are covariates in the detection function -- only when the
covariates vary at the scale of the observation. Transect-level
covariates like Beaufort sea state are fine to use count as the response
for. The way to think about it is: does the probability of detection
vary within segment? If it does, you need to use H-T (for now*), if
detectability only varies at the segment level, you can use count. I'm
working on a method of using count when detection covariates vary

2. I do recommend using the Tweedie in general as it can deal with the
various response types flexibly as it has continuous support.



Hope this helps.


--dave



* I'm working on a method of using count when detection covariates vary
within segment and will post something to the list once a preprint is ready.

Hi Kevin, hi listfolk,

That warning is safe to ignore if you know that the measurements are
correct -- dsm doesn't do any checking that the covariates don't vary at
the observation level, it just assumes that you are giving it reasonable
data. In a future version of dsm I'll put a more descriptive warning to
this effect.


cheers,
--dave
